body: Can you explain the rationale for these changes? A more comprehensive description would be useful since this touches a lot of sensitive code and has a high risk for regressions.

> Can you explain the rationale for these changes? A more comprehensive description would be useful since this touches a lot of sensitive code and has a high risk for regressions.

`poll()` is more modern than `select()`, offering better performance and security, without the 1024 file descriptor limit. The Wayland backend already uses `poll()` instead of `select()`.

To prevent unnecessary CPU usage, I changed the `_wait_for_events(0, 1000)` call from 1000 times per second to an indefinite sleep, and safely terminated it using the Self-Pipe Trick.

Before calling `poll()`, I added a check for `XEventsQueued` to immediately process buffered events. It's uncertain whether this will resolve the input delay issue, as I cannot reproduce #113188. I am awaiting testing from @Chestnut45.

Just built this branch and it unfortunately does re-introduce the dropped inputs issue described in #113188, which I think is too severe to allow back into the stable builds. I believe that any solution that allows the events thread to sleep for longer than 1x frametime (at any fps, minus a small margin) will reintroduce this issue.

I think that the most reasonable option to reduce CPU usage if the ~1% is too much to swallow, is to instead add a project setting like `allow_x11_events_thread_sleep` (maybe under Application -> Run ?) which when set to false (default), uses the current behaviour of a 1,000 microsecond timeout, but when true, uses the previous behaviour of a 1 second timeout (or indefinite, though I imagine the impact of polling once per second is almost certainly negligible). The option would have to include a description something along the lines of:

"Allowing the events polling thread to sleep reduces CPU usage by a small amount, but may cause delayed input processing that is undesirable for many types of games that rely on low input latency, though this may be acceptable for slower-paced games or non-game applications.

NOTE: This setting only affects Linux/X11 (however the documentation standards specify to format this information...)"

I don't yet have any experience adding project settings or reading them from other parts of the codebase, but if someone wants to implement that, I think it would only be a very small functional change on top of whatever is required to add the project setting (just changing the value passed to `_wait_for_events(timeout_seconds, timeout_microseconds)` **ONLY from the events thread polling loop, `DisplayServerX11::_poll_events()`**, based on the setting).

Thank you for the test. What do you think about directly reusing `run/low_processor_mode`? After all, if the user has enabled low processor mode, they are likely less concerned about rendering and input latency and more focused on performance consumption during idle times.

Hi, since `poll` and the self-pipe trick don't decrease latency, could you please switch back to the old code, so that the diff is smaller and easier to review? I think that just doing the trick of checking for low processor mode should be enough. Given the delicate situation with threading and such, the least changes we make the better.

FWIW, I think that at this point we might as well switch to an indefinite timeout in that case. Waiting for one second is waaaaay more than one frame anyways and I don't expect any difference in latency compared to an indefinite wait, with hopefully even less strain to the CPU.

(sorry for the double post)

That said, reintroducing latency in low-consumption modes might affect usability negatively, as some users complained non-smooth camera rotation with the old "slow" timeout. I'm afraid that this might make the editor jittery.

Oh, I must not have fully registered that last part on first glance, I wasn't aware that the editor uses `low_processor_mode`.

That does mean that reusing `low_processor_mode` for this would indeed cause the editor camera to stutter (as it already did since 4.5.1-stable and until 4.6-beta2 when the timeout was lowered, fixing it).

Since reusing `low_processor_mode` would re-introduce the input delay problem in the editor, I think having a separate project setting like in my first suggestion is the best option, and it has the added bonus of allowing users to still care about input latency when using low processor mode, which is clearly a valid use case since the Godot editor itself is one such case.

I don't think it makes a lot of sense to add a new project setting that introduces jittery movement and latency to save 0.2% CPU usage. Let's be realistic about what is actually needed for shipping applications and what tradeoffs are worth making. 

It's nice to be fully dedicated to avoiding any CPU costs whatsoever. But breaking out input handling to save a tiny bit of CPU usage is really not worth it. 

I would prefer to see a slight adjustment to the polling frequency instead. 1000 microseconds seems a bit small. We could probably get away with 3000-4000 even with 240hz monitors which would reduce the cost of polling by a factor of 3 to 4 without harming latency or introducing needless complexity

That does make sense to me, though anything above 2,000 would *most likely* re-introduce the stutter for 240hz, if I can get my hands on a higher refresh rate monitor I'll test that. I think that it's important to not raise the timeout without giving users an option, because there are plenty of games that would suffer from the input delay issue in a way that is important to gameplay (basically all rhythm games would have this issue), and lots of people like to play rhythm games at higher refresh rates to improve latency and increase the timing window. Users of the engine should be able to decide what trade-offs to make for their application, rather than the engine making that decision for them without any knowledge of what's important to the user. I'm not so worried about the CPU usage as I am about having an unfixable stutter (even if only at higher fps) without recompiling the engine, but it is worth mentioning that the real (unscaled) increase is closer to 2% on an i5-1240p, which is not entirely negligible. I am indeed quite sensitive to this because I have been optimizing the project's performance over the past few months. Suddenly, its idle CPU usage increased from 0.3% to 0.5%~0.6%, nearly doubling, which makes it hard for me to ignore.

I'm actually not in a hurry to solve this issue. I submitted the PR just to avoid forgetting about it later. Its current impact is minimal with limited to x11/xwayland, which is still tolerable.

Performance optimization is always like this—if you're not careful, you might introduce new performance costs that offset the gains from previous optimizations. A single performance cost might not be significant, but if left unchecked, it can accumulate over time to a point where it becomes impossible to ignore.
